attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The nearby Chamath quote is separate and is not part of this claim.

semantics.note: The 'appear' wording keeps his hedge ('doesn't seem'). It sits inside a rhetorical question ('Who is actually getting a profit?'). This is an appearance-based, graded-confidence statement, not a firm assertion.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading to hedged language, which policy does not allow. It also supplies its own terms: AI-attributable profit, the Q4 2025 period and cost allocation. The contract itself says no money verdict is possible without an accounting basis.

evidence.note: Amazon's own Q4 2025 disclosure. AWS segment operating income includes non-AI business, so it says nothing about AI-specific profit.
Microsoft's own FY26 Q2 disclosure (Oct–Dec 2025). The Intelligent Cloud margin is an aggregate figure and does not separate out AI profitability.

reviews.rationale: 'Doesn't seem' is hedged, graded-confidence language inside a rhetorical question, so policy says it is not scored. Even if it were scored, neither evidence item separates AI-attributable profit, and the contract itself rules out a verdict without an accounting basis.

attribution.note: He states the outage cause in his own voice. The FT sign-off detail is explicitly credited to the FT and is not part of the normalised claim.

semantics.note: The claim correctly isolates his firm causal assertion: multiple AWS outages caused by Kiro. Leaving out the meeting and sign-off clauses is reasonable; they are separate assertions.

contract.note: Reading 'multiple' as at least two and 'caused' as material contribution is ordinary and generous. When incident records are unavailable, the contract allows attributed reporting.

evidence.note: Reporting citing FT sources says Kiro contributed to one December 2025 AWS outage, with Amazon's denial included. This covers only one incident.
Reporting of the same FT story puts the second incident on Amazon Q Developer, not Kiro. That is a different tool, which matches the contract's contradiction example.
Amazon's own statement denies any second AWS event and blames access-control error. As a company disclosure it is not an independent finding.
Amazon's own clarification, dated before the post, says the March incidents involved retail systems, not AWS. It does not add any Kiro outage at AWS.

reviews.rationale: Only one AWS outage linked to Kiro is reported, and Amazon disputes it. The reporting most favourable to the claim ties the second incident to Amazon Q Developer, and Amazon denies a second AWS event at all. No source in the packet gives two Kiro-caused outages, so 'multiple outages caused by Kiro' fails. A single Kiro-linked incident remains plausible.

semantics.note: 'These companies' means Anthropic and OpenAI, and the 'don't really appear to' hedge is kept. This is an appearance-based, graded-confidence claim.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading to hedged language ('don't really appear to'), which policy forbids. It also supplies its own cost baseline, magnitude and accounting basis.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own October 2025 statement on its multi-chip strategy. It names an efficiency approach but gives no measured company cost savings.
Anthropic's own March 2025 post on token savings for customers. It measures customers' token use, not either company's own costs.

reviews.rationale: The claim is hedged ('don't really appear to'), so policy says it is not scored. In any case the packet has no matched measurement of either company's cost reductions, so even an unhedged reading would be unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Would immediately price out' is firm wording that depends on a hypothetical price rise of at least 300% (to $80 from $20). The antecedent is kept.

contract.note: The reading is fair and ordinary: the base $20 plan rises to at least $80; 'most' means a majority; 'just about every' means nearly all. A new premium tier does not count as meeting the condition.

evidence.note: A secondary price check dated Oct 26, 2026, before the cutoff, shows Pro still at $20 a month. No qualifying price increase is shown.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast. The packet shows no base-price increase to $80; the Pro price was still $20 in late October 2026. The antecedent has not happened, so policy says the forecast is not scored.
